For anyone who takes cards and has never read the statement

How much of your card bill is the processor, and how much is the network?

Five numbers off one merchant statement. This splits the fee into the part the card networks set — which no processor can discount — and the part your processor keeps, which is the only half a quote can change. Then it prices the same month under a competing quote.

What is a good effective rate?

Last month’s statement

Tapped, dipped or swiped in front of you. The rest is keyed or online, which genuinely costs more at the network level — an estimate is fine.

Statement, PCI compliance, gateway, batch, monthly minimum. Printed apart from the rate summary, which is why they are the easiest line to miss.

Compare against a quote

Defaults are a competitive interchange-plus quote for a small merchant. Replace them with whatever you have actually been offered.

What the statement says

3.10%effective rate
$0.93average fee per transaction
$951.30estimated network pass-through range $867.30 – $1,059.45
$348.70estimated processor markup range $240.55 – $432.70

    Common questions

    Which five numbers do I need off the statement?

    Total card sales for the month, the number of card transactions, the total fees charged, roughly what share of your sales were card-present (tapped, dipped or swiped in front of you) rather than keyed or online, and the flat monthly fees — statement, PCI, gateway, batch, monthly minimum. The first three are on the summary page of every statement. The fourth you can usually estimate from how the business runs. The fifth is the one people miss, because it is printed apart from the rate summary.

    Why does the tool refuse to give a single markup number?

    Because it cannot see your card mix, and the card mix moves interchange by more than a percentage point. A regulated debit card, a consumer credit card and a small-business rewards card run on the same terminal cost very different amounts, and nothing on a bundled statement tells you the split. So the estimate is a band. If you take a figure to your processor, take the band and say where it came from — a precise number you cannot defend is worse in that conversation than an honest range.

    What is interchange, and why can no processor discount it?

    Interchange is the portion the card-issuing bank keeps, set by the card networks on published schedules that apply identically to every merchant in a category. Assessments are a smaller slice the networks themselves keep. Together they are pass-through: your processor collects them and hands them on. Nobody sells them to you cheaper, which is why a quote that undercuts a competitor is always undercutting the third component — the processor’s own markup — and why splitting the bill is the only way to see whether a quote is actually better.

    Are the fixed monthly fees really markup?

    In substance, yes. A statement fee, a PCI-compliance fee, a gateway fee, a batch fee and a monthly minimum are all revenue the processor keeps, and none of them fall when your rate falls. On a business doing $42,000 a month they are easy to wave off as small; at $45 a month they are $540 a year, and they are the part of a bill most often left out of a rate comparison entirely. Price them separately when you compare quotes, because a quote that wins on rate and loses on monthly fees can cost more.

    My effective rate came out below the estimate. What does that mean?

    That the whole bill is explained by the cheapest reading of network pass-through, so this model cannot identify markup in it. That is usually good news, and it is occasionally a sign that a fee is being billed somewhere the total you entered does not include — an equipment lease on a separate invoice, or a fee netted out of deposits rather than charged monthly. Worth a look before concluding the account is cheap.

    Does a lower effective rate always mean a better deal?

    No, and this is the trap flat-rate pricing depends on. Effective rate divides fees by sales, so it is driven by your average ticket as much as by your pricing. A business with a $10 average ticket and a business with a $200 average ticket paying identical processor markup will show wildly different effective rates, because the per-transaction cents are spread over very different amounts. Compare the markup figure and the per-transaction fee, not the blended rate.

    Is any of this uploaded?

    No. The calculation runs entirely in your browser, there are no accounts, no cookies and no analytics vendor, and there is no network request in the page at all. A saved audit stores only the numbers you typed and stays in this browser; reset deletes it. Monthly card volume is effectively your revenue, which is exactly why none of it leaves the page.

    What should I actually ask my processor?

    Ask for interchange-plus pricing quoted as a percentage over interchange plus a per-transaction amount, and ask for every recurring monthly fee listed by name. Then ask them to price your last statement under that quote. If they will not put the markup and the monthly fees in writing as separate line items, you cannot compare their offer to anyone else’s — which is generally the reason it is not offered that way.

    This tool vs. Helcim’s Rate Calculator — a single vendor’s forward quote vs. an audit of the statement you already have.

vs-comparing-effective-rates.html.text:
← Card processing fee audit

This tool vs. comparing effective rates

The standard advice for shopping card processing is to collect a few quotes, divide each one's fees by sales, and take the lowest effective rate. It is easy to do and it is what almost every "how to shop your processor" article recommends. It is also the reason "shop your rate" advice is often noise: effective rate is driven by your average ticket as much as by the pricing itself, so it ranks quotes by a number your own business distorts, not by the markup you would actually pay.

Two merchants on character-for-character identical processor pricing will show effective rates nearly a full percentage point apart if one has a $10 average ticket and the other a $200 one, because the flat per-transaction cents spread over very different amounts of sales. Compare effective rates across two different quotes on your business and the distortion runs the other way too: a quote with a lower percentage and a higher per-transaction fee can look cheaper or more expensive purely from where the two components happen to land on your ticket size.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What's my current effective rate? Either one — total fees divided by total sales is arithmetic, not analysis.
Is a lower quoted effective rate actually cheaper on my own volume and ticket size? This tool — it re-prices your statement's actual volume and transaction count under the competing quote, in dollars, instead of comparing two blended percentages.
How much of my bill is network interchange nobody can discount, versus my processor's own markup? This tool's pass-through and markup bands — effective rate alone cannot separate the two.
Are the flat monthly fees (statement, PCI, gateway, batch) folded into the comparison? This tool — they are priced as their own line item on both sides. A bare effective-rate comparison usually ignores them.
Does the comparison need my current processor's rate sheet? No, on either — but this tool estimates pass-through from your volume and card-present share, so it never needs it.
Audit your own statement

This tool needs no account and nothing installed: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and your numbers stay on your device — there is no network request in the page at all, so nothing about your card volume is ever sent anywhere.

Common questions

Isn't comparing effective rates the standard way to shop processors?

It is the standard advice, and it is easy to follow: divide fees by sales for each quote and pick the lowest. The problem is not the arithmetic, it is what the number contains. Effective rate blends a percentage-of-sales component with a flat per-transaction fee, so two processors charging identical markup will show different effective rates on the same merchant if the quotes carry different per-transaction fees — and the same processor will show different effective rates on two merchants with different average tickets, even at identical pricing.

So a lower effective rate on a quote doesn't mean a better deal?

Not by itself. A quote with a lower percentage and a higher per-transaction fee can cost more on a business with a low average ticket and less on one with a high average ticket, and effective rate alone does not show you which. This tool separates the pass-through every processor charges from the markup that is actually negotiable, then re-prices your own statement's volume and transaction count under a competing quote, so the comparison is a dollar figure on your own mix rather than two blended percentages from two different merchants' worth of pricing.

Do I need to know my current processor's exact pricing structure to compare quotes this way?

No. You need five numbers off a statement you already have — card sales, transaction count, total fees, roughly what share was card-present, and the flat monthly fees — and the markup percentage, per-transaction fee, and monthly fees of the quote you are comparing against. The tool estimates network pass-through from the volume and mix, so it never needs your current processor's rate sheet.

Does this page recommend a specific processor?

No. It names no processor, and the comparison field accepts whatever markup, per-transaction fee, and monthly fees any quote states — there is nothing here that favors one company's pricing over another's.

vs-helcim-rate-calculator.html.text:
← Card processing fee audit

This tool vs. Helcim's Rate Calculator

Helcim publishes a free Rate Calculator on its pricing page: pick a country and industry, enter a projected monthly card volume and average transaction size, and it estimates what Helcim's own interchange-plus pricing would charge — currently interchange plus 0.40% plus 8¢ in person and interchange plus 0.50% plus 25¢ online, tiered down further as volume grows. It is forward-looking and single-vendor: a quote for a Helcim account that does not exist yet, built from numbers you project rather than numbers you already have.

That makes Helcim's tool the right choice for "what would Helcim specifically charge me." This tool answers a different question: for the statement you already have, from whichever processor issued it, how much of the bill is network interchange nobody can discount and how much is that processor's own markup — so you can judge the account you are actually on, not a projection from one vendor you have not switched to.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What would Helcim specifically charge for volume I have not run yet? Helcim's own Rate Calculator.
Of the bill I already have, from any processor, how much is unavoidable network cost and how much is markup? This tool's pass-through and markup bands.
Is a competing interchange-plus quote — Helcim's published rate or anyone else's — actually better on my own volume? This tool's re-priced comparison, using the same pass-through estimate for both quotes.
Do I need to pick an industry, project a future volume, or share who my processor is? No, for this tool. Helcim's calculator asks for the first two to build its quote.
Audit your own statement

This tool needs no account and no industry classification: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and your numbers stay on your device — there is no network request in the page at all, so nothing about your card volume is ever sent anywhere, including to Helcim or any other processor.

Common questions

What is the difference between this tool and Helcim's Rate Calculator?

Helcim's Rate Calculator is a sales quote tool: you enter your country, industry, projected monthly card volume and average transaction size, and it estimates what Helcim itself would charge you under its own interchange-plus pricing, in-person and online. It answers what one specific vendor would charge for volume you have not run yet. This tool answers a different question: for a statement you already have, from whichever processor issued it, how much is network interchange nobody can discount and how much is that processor's own markup and monthly fees, so you can judge the bill you are actually paying rather than a projection from a single vendor.

Does this tool require picking an industry or projecting future volume like Helcim's calculator does?

No. It reads five numbers off a statement for a month that already happened — card sales, transaction count, total fees, the card-present share, and the flat monthly fees — and never asks which processor issued it or what industry the business is in. Helcim's calculator instead needs a projected monthly volume and average ticket to price a Helcim account that does not exist yet.

Can I use Helcim's own published rates inside this tool?

Yes. Helcim publishes interchange-plus pricing starting at interchange plus 0.40% plus 8 cents in person and interchange plus 0.50% plus 25 cents online. Enter those as the competing quote's markup fields and this tool re-prices your actual statement's volume under them, on the same pass-through estimate as your current bill, so the two numbers you are comparing are the two processors' markups rather than two different pass-through assumptions.

Is this page affiliated with Helcim?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Helcim Inc. Helcim and Rate Calculator are named here only to describe what this tool is for and how the two differ.

To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use. Helcim's published rates are quoted from its own pricing page as of this writing and change at Helcim's discretion — verify the current figure on helcim.com before relying on it, and this tool's own pass-through estimate is a band, not a lookup of the rates on any account.

what-is-a-good-effective-rate-for-card-p.text:
← Card processing fee audit

What is a good effective rate for card processing?

It is the wrong question, and asking it is how most small businesses end up comparing two quotes on the one number that cannot tell them apart. The effective rate is total fees divided by total card sales, so it moves with your average ticket and your card mix at least as much as it moves with your pricing.

Open the free card processing fee audit

The same pricing, two very different rates

Take two businesses on identical processor pricing — interchange plus 0.25% plus $0.10 a transaction — running $42,000 of card sales in a month.

 CaféContractor
Average ticket$10$200
Transactions4,200210
Per-transaction fees at $0.10$420$21
Effect on the blended rate+1.00%+0.05%

Nearly a full percentage point of difference, from pricing that is character-for-character the same. Any advice of the form “anything over 2.9% is too high” is, on these two businesses, right once and wrong once by accident.

The three components, and which one is yours to argue about

Interchange is the portion the card-issuing bank keeps. The card networks publish the schedules; they apply identically to every merchant in a category, and no processor sells them to you cheaper.

Assessments are a smaller slice the networks themselves keep — roughly a tenth of a percent plus a couple of cents. Also pass-through, also not negotiable.

Processor markup is everything left over: the percentage and per-transaction fee the processor adds, plus every recurring monthly fee. This is the entire negotiable surface, and on a bundled statement it is the one number nobody prints.

What to do with one statement

  1. Take total card sales, transaction count and total fees off the summary page.
  2. Estimate what share of sales were taken in person rather than keyed or online — card-not-present interchange is genuinely higher, and that part is not your processor’s to give back.
  3. Add up the flat monthly lines: statement, PCI compliance, gateway, batch, monthly minimum.
  4. Split the bill into pass-through and markup, then price the same month under any quote you have been offered. A quote that will not state its markup and monthly fees as separate line items cannot be compared to anything.

The card processing fee audit does the arithmetic in your browser — nothing is uploaded, which matters here because monthly card volume is effectively your revenue.

Common questions

What is a good effective rate for credit card processing?

There is no single good number, for the reason the table above shows. The comparable figures are the processor’s markup over interchange and the flat monthly fees.

How do I work out my effective rate?

Divide one month’s total fees by that month’s total card sales. $1,300 on $42,000 is 3.10%. Include the flat monthly lines in the fee total — leaving them out is how a rate that looks competitive turns out not to be.

What part of my processing bill can actually be negotiated?

The processor’s markup and the recurring monthly fees. Interchange and assessments are pass-through, collected on behalf of the issuing bank and the network.

Is flat-rate pricing more expensive than interchange-plus?

Usually, and the gap grows with volume — but not always. Flat-rate charges one number for every card, so a business whose customers mostly pay by debit is subsidising one whose customers mostly pay by rewards card. Price your own statement both ways before switching.

What are the monthly fees on a merchant statement for?

They are processor revenue, and they do not fall when your rate does. At $45 a month they are $540 a year, which is worth pricing as its own line rather than rounding away.
